newsitem.title: SPAIN: Iberia bond spreads seen resting for summer siesta.
newsitem.headline: Iberia bond spreads seen resting for summer siesta.

text.p: Iberian bonds are unlikely to awake next week from their summer siesta, a slumber which only September or even October 1998 budget news may be able to disturb, analysts said on Friday.
After a week of treading water, Spanish bonos and their Portuguese counterparts have become lethargic.

"Although one can be very bullish on Spain, there is no immediate reason to buy. I do not see that much scope for another fall (in the spread between bonos and Bunds)," said Francesco Giordano, economist at CSFB in London.
But there is also no reason to sell.
Technically, implicit five-year forward rates are even lower than cash, making financing of positions in the long-end costly until the short-end falls, Giordano added.
Since the Bank of Spain seems to have put on hold any further relaxation of its monetary policy, the market has to wait to see any relevant change.

"The (cash) spread over Bunds found very strong resistance at 60 basis points. Next week, it could climb toward 70, but I do not expect any major movement in short run," said Valentin Fernandez economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
The Spanish 10-year cash spread versus Bunds, which hit a record low at 60 basis points on June 19, traded this morning near 66 basis points.
Spain's CPI, which rose 1.6 percent year on year in June versus May's 1.5 percent, confirmed the sharp decline in the Spanish inflation had bottomed.

The end of the inflation downtrend together with a recovery of economic activity seemed to suggest the Spanish central bank would be prudent, analysts said. And the Bank of Portugal is likely to adopt a similar approach for the near-term.
"We think the Bank of Portugal has plenty of room for further cuts, but given the fact inflation seems sticky, they would prefer to wait," one analyst with a major Portuguese bank in Lisbon said.
Portugual's June CPI is due on Monday, and forecasts range between 2.0 percent and 2.4 percent, after May's 2.1 percent.
The Portuguese 10-year cash spread over Bunds, trading at around 72 basis points after a minimum at around 50 basis points at the end of May also reflected political concerns.
Prime Minister Antonio Guterres threatened to resigne ten days ago.

Analysts said the Portuguese spread had climbed above its Spanish counterpart mainly because it had become increasingly clear Portugal, with Spain, would be part of Europe's single currency from its start.

"It's now sure that if Portugal will make it, it will make it with Spain," said Fernandez. "So, there is no reason for staying with a bigger presence in a less-liquid market, such as the Portuguese one, instead of in Spain."
A similar argument can be applied to differences between Spain and Italy, analysts said.
Recently, bonos lagged Italy's market, whose spread versus Bunds fell sharply in the last month.
The differential between Spanish and Italian 10-year yields was around 28 basis points on Friday versus about 65 basis points in mid-June.
"The Spanish spread has found a point of equilibrium. Italian market is close to it," said Giordano.
